title: The ledger of hours
hookLine: we guard our money closely and hand out our time to anyone who asks

cards: A stranger asks for twenty dollars, no reason. The answer is no, probably without a thought.
A stranger asks for twenty minutes: a survey, a sales call, a meeting that could have been an email, a video that autoplays into the next. Those get handed over all day long.
Seneca noticed the same strange double standard, in yesterday's essay. We guard our money. We give our time to anyone who asks.

teach.b: In the essay's third chapter, people won't let anyone take an inch of their land, Seneca says. One boundary dispute and they're off to court, with stones and weapons.
But they let others walk right into their lives, and even invite them in. Nobody hands out their money; everybody hands out their life.
Tight-fisted with property, wildly generous with the one thing it would be right to be stingy with: time. Then a clever move.

He asks a man who's reached old age to go through the ledger. Take your years and subtract. How much went to a creditor, to a patron you had to flatter, to quarrels at home, to errands around the city?
Subtract all that, and you have fewer years than you counted.
In the first of his letters to his friend Lucilius, it's one line, in Richard Gummere's translation: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." A house can be taken, money lost.
Time is the one thing put in your hands alone, and the one thing nobody ever returns. He doesn't say never give it away. Friendship, service, love: those take hours, and they're worth it.
His point is the ledger. Know where it goes. Choose where it goes.
Guard at least one hour the way you'd guard your wallet.

how: People who follow Seneca's advice often keep an account of their time, as he told Lucilius he did, and deliberately protect some hours for what they value most.

games.q: Seneca asks an old man to go through the ledger of his life. what does he tell him to do with the years?
o: add up the money they earned.
subtract the time others took, and see what's left.
games.why: subtract the creditor, the patron, the quarrels, the errands. you'll find you have fewer years than you've counted.

practice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture tomorrow as a ledger, morning to evening, and notice which hours are already spoken for.
Then find one hour you'd truly choose to guard, for a walk, a friend, a book or rest, and picture yourself saying no, kindly, to what would take it.

wordCard.voice: Seneca. His reminder that we guard our money and give our time away, when time is all that's truly ours.

orig.note: Latin, from Seneca's first letter to Lucilius: only time is ours. The full line begins omnia, Lucili, aliena sunt, all things are someone else's.

carryVoice: Your line: time is the only property. It's the one thing put in your hands alone. Day thirty-one, done.

sources.ref: On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae) 3
